rationale: The book's core claim — that the gnashing of teeth in the judgment formula is the rage of the wicked directed at the righteous, provoked by the sight of the kingdom they forfeited — is carried better by the cited texts than the strongest specific alternative (gnashing as the anguish/pain of the condemned themselves). Every supplied occurrence of tooth-gnashing outside the formula (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Ps 35:16; Job 16:9; Lam 2:16; Acts 7:54) is hostility aimed at another person, never a sound of one's own pain; the anguish reading cannot produce a single text where gnashing expresses the gnasher's own suffering. Luke 13:28, the one Gospel occurrence that explains its own trigger, places the gnashing 'when ye shall see' the patriarchs inside — matching Psalm 112:10's exact sequence (see, be grieved, gnash, perish) element for element, which also accounts for the weeping/gnashing pairing (grieved = weeping, gnash = gnashing). Acts 7:54 stages the identical scene in narrative: the excluded gnashing while the righteous man sees the opened kingdom. The Matthew 24:51/Psalm 35:16 'hypocrites' link is a further specific cross-textual connection the anguish reading leaves unexplained. However, the entry's secondary elaborations — the annihilationist endpoint ('then they melt away' as the sentence executed), the Greek definite-article argument, and the Hebrew Matthew vocabulary claims — go beyond what the supplied evidence establishes and are not indispensable to the core identification, so support is CORE_ONLY.
book_core_identification: The gnashing of teeth in the 'weeping and gnashing' formula is the rage/hatred of the wicked directed at the righteous — the excluded insiders' reaction at the sight of the kingdom and the blessed within it — with the weeping as grief over their own loss; it is not a description of pain inflicted by torment.
book_secondary_elaborations: The Greek definite articles ('the weeping and the gnashing') mark a known, fixed scene the hearers were expected to recognize from the psalms.
The scene ends in dissolution rather than endless torment: Psalm 112:10's 'melt away... the desire of the wicked shall perish' completes the sentence (annihilationist implication).
The Hebrew Matthew renders the formula with charaq (the root of Ps 112:10) and names the destinations in grave-vocabulary (Gehinnom, lowest Sheol, dark places of the depths).
All seven who are cast out are insiders/claimants of the house, never heathen.
Matthew 24:51's 'portion with the hypocrites' links the evil servant's company to the 'hypocritical mockers' who gnash in Psalm 35:16.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The mainstream reading: 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' is a fixed Matthean/Lukan formula for the extreme anguish, despair, and remorse of the condemned under eschatological judgment — the conscious misery of exclusion (and, in fiery-furnace contexts, of torment). The gnashing on this reading expresses the sufferer's own pain and regret, not hostility toward the righteous; the OT rage-usages are a different idiom applied to living enemies of the righteous, whereas the Gospel formula describes the emotional state of the punished.
counter_core_identification: Gnashing of teeth signifies the anguish, despair, and remorseful suffering of those excluded and condemned — an expression of the condemned's own misery under judgment.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the gnashing is directed hostility toward the righteous; it asserts the gesture is the condemned's own pain and regret — the two cannot both be the primary identification of the same gesture, since the book expressly holds it is 'never once the sound of pain' but 'the face of hatred.'
counter_case: The formula is consistently attached to punishment imagery — outer darkness, the furnace of fire, being cut asunder — which naturally suggests suffering rather than defiance.

Pairing with 'weeping' pushes the whole phrase toward grief and misery; weeping is unambiguously sorrow, and a unified emotional reading (despair) is simpler than splitting the pair into two different emotions.
Luke 13:28's context of being 'thrust out' while others feast can be read as bitter regret over lost opportunity rather than hatred of those inside.
The OT rage-texts (Ps 35:16; 37:12; Job 16:9; Lam 2:16) describe living persecutors gnashing at victims, a social-hostility idiom that need not govern an eschatological punishment formula.
This is the dominant homiletical and commentarial gloss, treating the phrase as a stock picture of eschatological misery.
book_explanatory_advantages: Lexical uniformity: every supplied biblical occurrence of gnashing outside the formula is hostility aimed at another (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Ps 35:16; Job 16:9; Lam 2:16; Acts 7:54); the book's reading uses the word's established biblical meaning, while the counter requires the Gospel formula to coin a new sense with no attested parallel.

Psalm 112:10 supplies the complete template — the wicked sees (the blessing of the righteous), is grieved, gnashes, and perishes — exactly matching Luke 13:28's structure ('when ye shall see Abraham... and you yourselves thrust out'), including the weeping/gnashing pair (grieved/gnash).
Luke 13:28 ties the gnashing to a sight of the righteous inside the kingdom, not to torment being inflicted — the trigger the book's reading predicts and the anguish reading must treat as incidental.

Acts 7:54 provides a New Testament narrative enactment: the council gnashing at Stephen while he sees the glory of God and the opened heaven — the same tableau with roles reversed at the end of the age.
The Matthew 24:51 'portion with the hypocrites' / Psalm 35:16 'hypocritical mockers... gnashed' correspondence is a specific intertextual link only the book's reading exploits.

The observation that all seven cast-out figures are insiders (children of the kingdom, servants, wedding guests) coheres with the psalmic scene of claimants confronted by the vindication of the truly righteous.
counter_explanatory_advantages: A unified 'misery' reading of the weeping+gnashing pair is simpler than assigning two distinct emotions.
The furnace-of-fire settings (Matt 13:42, 50) sit naturally with pain-driven expression, and the counter needs no explanation for why a rage idiom appears in torment contexts.
It matches the overwhelming weight of interpretive tradition, so it requires no revision of received readings.
decisive_sources: Psalm 112:10 — the see/grieve/gnash/perish template matching the formula's structure and pairing
Psalm 37:12; Psalm 35:16; Job 16:9; Lamentations 2:16 — uniform biblical usage of gnashing as hostility at another, never one's own pain
Luke 13:28 — the gnashing occurs at the sight of the patriarchs in the kingdom, supplying the trigger
Acts 7:54 — New Testament narrative staging of gnashing at the righteous man who sees the opened kingdom
Matthew 24:51 with Psalm 35:16 — the 'hypocrites' link identifying the gnashing company
unresolved_objections: The annihilationist elaboration ('then they melt away'; five destination-names as 'vocabulary of the grave') extends Psalm 112:10's ending into eschatological doctrine — a step the supplied texts suggest but do not compel, and it engages the wider hell debate beyond this formula.
The Hebrew Matthew claims (charaq; Gehinnom; lowest Sheol readings of 'outer darkness') rest on a disputed textual witness not verifiable from the supplied excerpts.
The Greek definite-article argument is asserted but not demonstrated from supplied evidence.

The counter's simplicity point stands partially: the book must still allow that 'weeping' carries sorrow while 'gnashing' carries rage — two emotions in one formula — though Psalm 112:10 ('grieved... gnash') itself attests exactly that combination.
